title: Semantic Search Applications
learning_outcomes: Explain natural-language search and how it connects to semantic search applications.
Apply semantic faq retrieval in the example and predict the output before running it.
Test one realistic edge case for semantic search applications and explain what the example does not prove.

content.intro: This lesson covers semantic search applications through 6 syllabus subtopics preserved from the supplied Generative AI curriculum. Represent content as embeddings and build semantic or hybrid retrieval. Evaluate ranking with representative queries and preserve permissions through retrieval.
content.why_it_matters: Use natural-language search as a lens for understanding semantic search applications. Trace its inputs, the operation or decision it describes, the result a learner can observe, and the limitations that matter for the intended task. Confirm the idea with a small example and an explicit check rather than relying on fluent or plausible output.

items.title: Semantic FAQ retrieval
items.text: Semantic FAQ retrieval concerns how content is represented, selected, or ranked for relevance. Keep the source text and metadata traceable, measure retrieval with labeled queries, and verify that similarity scores correspond to useful results rather than assuming nearby vectors prove factual correctness.

content_blocks.title: Provider and version note
content_blocks.text: Model names, API payloads, supported modalities, quotas, pricing, and SDK behavior vary by provider and change over time. Treat linked official documentation as the authority for a live integration; examples here avoid hard-coded production model IDs and secrets.

content.task: Practice natural-language search within semantic search applications: use a small synthetic input, predict the result, run the example, then change one input to test an edge case. Record the expected result and one limitation.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example uses a clearly described, non-sensitive input.
Expected behavior and at least one edge/failure case are written down.
The learner checks the result against an explicit criterion and records limitations.
hints: Begin with a tiny input whose expected behavior you can explain before running it.
Change one variable at a time and retain a fixed baseline for comparison.
When a model or external service is involved, inspect evidence and errors; do not treat the model response as a trusted instruction.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming fluent or plausible output is necessarily correct.
common_mistakes.fix: Use evidence, schema checks, representative test cases, and human review for consequential results.

common_mistakes.mistake: Changing several inputs or parameters at once.
common_mistakes.fix: Keep a baseline and vary one factor at a time so the effect can be interpreted.

common_mistakes.mistake: Putting secrets or private source material in prompts, logs, or a public example.
common_mistakes.fix: Use synthetic data, server-side secret storage, data minimization, and reviewed retention rules.
